name: Juten-dofu (aseptic packed tofu)
text: Tofu made by pouring cold soy milk and coagulant straight into a container, sealing it and heating it so it sets inside the pack. Because setting and sterilising happen in one step, it keeps far longer than shop tofu. There is no water-soaking stage, so no cooling bath is involved.
flavor: Smooth, uniform set; some tasters notice a slight coagulant bitterness (egumi) because the curd is never rinsed in water.
use: Long-shelf-life retail and institutional tofu; chilled dishes and soups where uniform texture matters more than a hand-made bean flavour.
craft: The coagulant is dispersed in the cold soy milk before sealing, so dosing and mixing decide the whole texture; there is no later correction. Check pack seal and best-before date, and note that the sources reviewed do not give industrial temperatures or times.

name: Nigari (traditional tofu coagulant)
text: Nigari is the traditional coagulant for tofu; its main component is magnesium chloride. Other coagulants besides nigari are in use today, so a tofu is not necessarily nigari-set unless the maker says so. The name momen (cotton) or kinugoshi (silk) refers to how the curd is pressed or set, not to the coagulant.
flavor: Used in tofu making: gives a clean set; the sources reviewed do not describe flavour differences between coagulants.
use: Added to hot soy milk to set tofu; ask the maker which coagulant is used when you need to specify a spec.
craft: Coagulant choice and dosing are the central variable in tofu making; the sources reviewed give no dosing figures, so confirm ratios with the maker.
src: Yoga Journal Japan - momen and kinugoshi

name: Koya-dofu (freeze-dried tofu, Koyasan)
text: Freeze-dried tofu said to have been perfected on Mt Koya by the monk Mokujiki Ogo and spread through shojin cooking. The Koya name was used in the Kansai area. By the Edo period the product had split into two methods, natural-drying shimi-dofu and a type that is thawed and then dried. Today over 90 percent of production is in Nagano, and an artificial-freezing tofu was shown at the 5th Domestic Industrial Exposition in 1903.
flavor: Light, neutral, sponge-like body that takes up broth.
use: Simmered in dashi seasoned with soy and mirin; also egg-set dishes and shojin cooking.
craft: The sponge texture comes from freezing and dehydrating; mechanised production today keeps quality stable. Sources disagree on the exact legend and the spelling of dates, so treat Mokujiki Ogo origin as tradition.

name: Shimi-dofu / kori-dofu (naturally frozen tofu)
text: Freeze-preserved tofu known as shimi-dofu or kori-dofu in the Koshinetsu, Tohoku and Hokkaido regions, where it was a winter preservation food made by the same basic freezing method as Koya-dofu. In Nagano, cold winters long supported its making, and it is still cooked in home dishes such as shimi-dofu with egg.
flavor: Absorbent, light, slightly chewy sponge.
use: Simmered dishes and egg-set preparations (Nagano home cooking).
craft: Natural drying depends on cold, dry winter weather; the Edo-period split between natural drying and thaw-then-dry methods is recorded by a maker. The sources reviewed give no soak or simmer times.
src: JA Group - Nagano shimi-dofu with egg

name: Nama-fu (fresh wheat gluten)
text: Fresh fu is made by mixing wheat gluten, the protein left after washing the starch out of flour, with glutinous rice flour, then steaming or boiling it. Kyoto nama-fu is of this type. It is distinct from baked, dried yaki-fu, which uses wheat flour with the gluten.
flavor: Soft, springy, mochi-like chew with little taste of its own.
use: Grilled, deep-fried or simmered; served in soups and in kaiseki cooking.
craft: Texture is governed by the gluten to glutinous-rice-flour balance and by steaming versus boiling; the sources reviewed give no ratios, so confirm them with the maker.

name: Yaki-fu (baked dried fu)
text: Yaki-fu is made by adding wheat flour to wheat gluten, baking it and drying it. Fu overall divides by method into nama-fu, yaki-fu and fried fu. All share gluten as the main ingredient. Regional forms such as kuruma-fu and Shonai-fu are baked types.
flavor: Dry, light and absorbent; mild wheat taste once soaked.
use: Restored in water and used in miso soup, simmered dishes and sukiyaki-style pots.
craft: Wheat flour is added to the gluten so the dough puffs when baked and gives a light bite. Restoration time depends on the shape; the sources reviewed give no figures.

name: Kuruma-fu (wheel fu)
text: A baked fu made by washing strong flour to remove starch, mixing a little flour back into the gluten, stretching it thin and winding it around an iron bar of about 2 m, then turning and baking it before drying. Types are split into two-wind and three-to-four-wind systems: two-wind is mainly made in Okinawa and Yamagata, three or more winds mainly in Niigata.
flavor: Spongy and absorbent, with a crisp-to-tender bite depending on soaking.
use: Restored and simmered, or dipped in egg and fried as a cutlet-style dish.
craft: The added flour makes the sheet puff and gives a crisp texture when baked. The number of windings determines the type, so specify it when ordering.

name: Shonai-fu / ita-fu (plank fu)
text: Plank-shaped baked fu made from the same dough as kuruma-fu: it is baked, then pressed flat into a board. Main production areas named in the sources are Yamagata and Akita prefectures.
flavor: Dry, light, absorbent board that softens into a mild wheat body.
use: Soaked and used in simmered dishes, soups and local home cooking.
craft: A product of kuruma-fu dough, so the gluten-to-flour balance and baking determine the finish. The sources reviewed give no further process figures.

name: Ita-konnyaku and tama-konnyaku (block and ball konnyaku)
ja: 板こんにゃく・玉こんにゃく
text: Block konnyaku is shaped and set with a board or mould; tama-konnyaku is rolled by hand without a mould and boiled. Gunma accounts for most Japanese konjac harvest: 49,700 t in Reiwa 6, about 97 percent of the national total, centred on Showa village and the Shimonita area. The Japan Konnyaku Association page lists the types.
flavor: Neutral, firm and springy; a faint alkaline note is removed by blanching.
use: Simmered (oden, nimono), stir-fried, or as sashimi-style slices.
craft: Konjac flour-based product (white) versus whole-tuber product (darker with skin flecks). Pre-blanch to remove alkali smell. Production statistics vary by year and source.

name: Nama-imo konnyaku (whole-tuber konnyaku)
text: Konnyaku made directly from fresh konjac tubers rather than dried flour. Skin is included, so the colour is greyer than white flour-based konnyaku. A producer describes heating gently from low temperature, which needs less coagulant. Home recipes from Gunma use soda ash or slaked lime.
flavor: Greyish with flecks, more tuber aroma and a softer, tender bite than flour-based block.
use: Simmered or eaten as sashimi with miso or ginger soy.
craft: Slow low-temperature heating is cited as the method; coagulant is calcium or soda-based. The sources reviewed give no ratios, so a professional should fix them by trial.

name: Seiko (konjac flour)
text: Konnyaku was first made from fresh tubers; in the Edo period a method using refined dried konjac flour (seiko) was developed, enabling year-round production and spreading the craft across the country. Seiko-based konnyaku is white, and the common industrial method is called the Odo system, using calcium hydroxide as coagulant.
flavor: Used in making: yields white, clean-tasting konnyaku.
use: Raw material for most commercial block, shirataki and ball konnyaku.
craft: Whiteness signals refined flour; whole-tuber products are greyer from skin. Coagulant is calcium hydroxide in the Odo method, per a maker's description.

name: Odawara kamaboko (steamed itatsuki kamaboko)
text: Steamed kamaboko mounted on a wooden board, made mainly from guchi (croaker). MAFF describes the sequence: remove the flesh, wash in water to remove oil and blood, dewater, grind with salt in a stone mortar and season, then strain to remove small bones and skin. The seasoned paste is mounded on a board and steamed.
flavor: Elastic, clean white-fish sweetness.
use: Sliced as appetiser, in soba and oden; New Year osechi.
craft: Salt-grinding develops the elastic gel (ashi); thorough washing removes oil and blood; straining removes bones. Treat the exact proportions as maker-specific.

name: Sasa-kamaboko (Sendai bamboo-leaf kamaboko)
text: A grilled kamaboko from Sendai shaped like a bamboo leaf. Sources name flounder, kichiji (kinki) and itoyori-type fish as raw materials, grilled over charcoal. Its origin is given as the flounder paste sold in leaf shape in the early Meiji era from Sendai Bay catches.
flavor: Browned surface, springy and sweet from white fish.
use: Eaten as is, lightly warmed, with wasabi soy.
craft: Species mix and charcoal grilling define the product; the account of its origin is traditional and details differ between sources.

name: Uwajima jakoten
text: A fried fish cake from Uwajima, Ehime, made by grinding small fish from Uwa Sea, especially hotaru-jako (called haranbo locally), with the bones, then frying. Uwajima kamaboko making is traditionally dated to 1615 when Date Hidemune is said to have brought Sendai kamaboko craftsmen with him, but this is one account among others.
flavor: Rustic, strong fish flavour, slightly gritty from bones.
use: Eaten warm, with ginger or grated daikon and soy; lightly grilled.
craft: Whole-fish paste with bones gives roughness rather than the clean gel of white-fish kamaboko. Freshness of small fish matters; check origin and frying oil quality.

name: Satsuma-age / tsukeage (fried fish cake)
ja: さつま揚げ・つけあげ
text: Fried kamaboko, called satsuma-age in Tokyo and tsukeage in Kagoshima. One etymology links tsukeage with Ryukyuan chikiagi. The sources reviewed do not give recipe ratios.
flavor: Sweet, fried, fish-forward with seasoning.
use: Eaten warm, simmered in oden or stir-fries.
craft: Name varies by region; confirm what product is meant when ordering. Etymology is a theory.

name: Tottori tofu-chikuwa
text: A steamed chikuwa of eastern Tottori made by mixing momen tofu and white-fish paste, commonly said to be about 7 to 3. The origin story credits the lord Ikeda Mitsunaka with urging people to eat tofu in place of scarce fish, though sources differ on the lord's name. There is no formal standard for the ratio. Unlike the usual grilled chikuwa, it is steamed, giving a white, soft body.
flavor: White, fluffy, mild, with soybean sweetness and fish savour.
use: Eaten sliced with ginger soy, grilled, or in oden.
craft: Salt is added in small amounts for elasticity. The 7:3 ratio is customary rather than official. Several makers exist in eastern Tottori.

name: Date-maki (rolled egg and fish paste)
text: A sweet osechi item made from white-fish paste with egg and dashi, baked and rolled on a bamboo mat while hot to show a swirl. Origins are disputed: one tradition ties it to Date Masamune hira-tamago-yaki, another to the Nagasaki castella-kamaboko, and the Yaizu cooperative says it began with flounder meat mixed with egg and baked.
flavor: Sweet, soft, eggy, with a springy fish-paste background.
use: New Year osechi, sliced in rounds.
craft: Paste ground with salt, liquid egg added, then heated and shaped; roll while hot. The Yaizu account describes the process but gives no ratios.
src: Kamaboko no Aru Kurashi - datemaki origin

name: Naruto-maki
text: A kamaboko in which seasoned paste is spread thin, a red-coloured paste placed in the centre, then rolled with an onisudare mat and boiled; the cut face shows a whirlpool, the source of the name. Hawaiian versions have a red edge, thought to follow the form carried by Meiji-Taisho emigrants.
flavor: Mild kamaboko, mainly decorative.
use: Topping for ramen and noodle soups.
craft: The spiral comes from the rolled-up thin sheet; cut across the roll to show the pattern.

name: Hanpen
text: A soft fish-paste cake; its fluffy texture is created by whipping air into the paste together with egg white and yamaimo (mountain yam), according to the Kibun product encyclopedia.
flavor: Very soft, airy and mild.
use: Oden, soups, grilled with butter or soy.
craft: Handle gently; heat only briefly or it collapses and loses the fluffy bite.

name: Tofuyo (Okinawan fermented tofu)
text: Firm shima-dofu dried and then aged for several months (4 to 5 months in one account) in a bed of rice koji, red koji and awamori. It is said to descend from Chinese furu (fermented tofu) brought in the Ryukyu Kingdom era; unlike the salt-cured Chinese form, awamori is used. Red-koji tofuyo is red and ranked above yellow-koji.
flavor: Likened to a mix of awamori and Edam cheese, or to sea urchin; the tofu taste fades as it ages.
use: Tiny pieces eaten with awamori, taken on a toothpick.
craft: Protein breakdown during ageing drives the creamy texture. Origin is debated; verify koji type (red or yellow) with the maker.

name: Kumiage-yuba (scooped fresh yuba)
text: Fresh yuba is the film formed on heated soy milk; the two fresh types are kumiage and hikiage. For kumiage the film is scooped from the pan. Home guides cite a film starting to form around 70 C, kept at 70-80 C without boiling. A Kyoto tofu shop says tsumami yuba is let form for 3-4 minutes and maki yuba for 13-14 minutes.
flavor: Creamy and soft, with the gentle sweetness of soy milk.
use: Eaten fresh with wasabi and soy or ponzu.
craft: Do not boil: the surface must form slowly. Soy milk concentration is adjusted by the shop; sources reviewed give no exact Brix.
src: Kamo Tofu - how to make yuba

name: Hikiwari natto (cut-bean natto)
text: Natto made from soybeans that are roasted, cracked and dehulled before fermentation. The greater surface area makes the savour come through more and the lack of hulls gives a softer texture.
flavor: Soft, with stronger savour than whole-bean natto.
use: Mixed over rice, in soups and rolls.
craft: Different from whole-bean natto in its preparation; home guides note the process differs from ordinary natto.

name: Shiokara-natto (salty koji natto)
text: Natto is classed into stringy natto fermented by Bacillus natto and non-stringy salty natto fermented by koji mould. Stringy types include whole-bean, hikiwari and gotō-type. The sources reviewed do not describe individual temple natto in detail.
flavor: Salty and dry, not sticky.
use: Seasoning-like side or flavouring.
craft: Koji mould, not natto bacteria; regional names such as temple natto were not detailed in the sources reviewed.

name: Natto fermentation parameters
text: Traditional: steamed soybeans wrapped in rice straw and kept at about 40 C for about a day, the straw supplying the bacteria. Industrial: pure-cultured natto bacteria sprayed on steamed soybeans, held at 40-42 C; heat builds over about 6 hours, cooled after 18-24 hours to stop fermentation. Soaking time depends on water temperature: about 24 h winter, 15 h spring/autumn, 6 h summer (home guide).
flavor: Process note.
use: Reference for making and judging natto.
craft: Fermentation needs oxygen, so lids should not be fully sealed; cooling halts fermentation. Home figures are guides rather than industrial specs.
